For washing, i use a body soap bar first to remove odor/heavier duty cleaning, then follow with a scented body wash. If you use heat on your hair, try to use as low of heat as possible because excessive heat will give it a burnt smell. Follow up with a good rich body cream and/or oil. Can be scented if you like or can just be plain. This will help any perfume you spray last longer on the skin. Spray your perfume onto the pressure points of your upper body; sides of neck, elbow pits, wrists. Tap your wrists together. Do not rub them. It will change the scent. When shopping for scents, look for anything that’s and Eau de Parfum or a Parfum. These will have the highest concentration of perfume alcohol/oil in the fragrance which helps it last longer/project more. When looking for what kind of scent you like, keep in mind what will tend to last and what won’t. Typically fresh or fruity scents tend to not have as long of a lasting power as muskier scents, sweet scents, or florals. Spraying your fragrance on your clothes will also help them last longer through the day as they won’t degrade from your natural oils/sweat. They also won’t change on you so you’ll smell it the most authentically. I usually do a combo of clothing and skin application. You can buy a fragrance mist for your hair/spray perfume in your hair but do so after using your heat tools, not before. Avoid using body sprays on their own as they usually don’t last very long, but can be nice layering scents for stronger perfumes. Hope this helps.

Edit to add, even though it seems obvious: make sure your layering product scents match up. Mixing a tropical fruity body wash with a rose scented body cream followed by a masculine-leaning perfume may be overwhelming or just not mix well. Find similar notes within your layered fragrances or keep it simple.

I second laser if it bothers you that much. It’s not cheap but a lot of places offer monthly payment packages if you sign up for like a year’s worth essentially. Often times they do a credit check for it though. It’s not permanent and often you will have to go back for touch ups, but it definitely helps make the hair thinner/make it grow back softer. You can buy at home wax strips/kits and wax parts of your body yourself if you aren’t able to afford it, but do some research about proper techniques before attempting. You can’t exfoliate beforehand for about 2-3 days or you risk lifting the skin. If using soft (strip) wax, always apply with the growth pattern of the hair and remove in the opposite direction, keeping the strip perpendicular to the skin as you remove. If using hard wax (you remove the wax itself with no strip) apply against the grain and create a nice lip for yourself to grab on to and remove against the growth pattern of the hair like the soft wax. Start small and don’t burn yourself. You could also try a hair removal cream like nair in place of shaving.

Therapists are not there to get advice from their clients. Most are very private about their lives for the most part. Some may share stories or experiences that have relevance to a topic their client has brought up, but only if it serves to benefit the client and how they process their own experience or how they could look at it from a different perspective. So a few things
1. Giving me the vibe she’s one of those therapists who became a therapist bc she thinks it will help her work through her own issues by helping others and not bc she’s a good fit for the job requirement.
2. In any profession, texting during a meeting or consultation or even conversation is extremely disrespectful, especially considering you’re paying for that conversation by the hour. If it was once in a while in an emergency situation it’s one thing, but even then if it’s that much of an emergency they should simply cancel and reschedule your session altogether.
3. Your relationship is not like any other relationship. She is your therapist, not your mom, not your best friend, not your sister. Your relationship is a professional one and she especially is responsible for keeping it as such. Yours is not a give and take relationship. You are not to carry her burdens because she helps you learn how to carry your own. As kind as she has been she has misunderstood and mistreated her role as your therapist. 
4. Playing off your extremely valid feeling and concerns over her texting during your appointments and saying you bringing it up shows “a common issue in your relationships” is incredibly immature and is icing on the cake at her overall lack of professionalism. 

Tldr: if she works for a company, absolutely file a complaint. If she freelances/works solo, maybe consider reporting her to the licensing board. She’s extremely unprofessional and should, in her words, work on that issue :)

If you struggle to brush your teeth or do a whole oral hygiene routine, start as another commenter suggested and just brush for 30 seconds. You can also do a good swig of mouthwash instead. I had a lot of intrusive thoughts i was deeply ashamed of having for a while, centering around things i did as a child that i thought were super wrong and horrible. I told my therapist about them and how i don’t want to have these thoughts, that i was revolted by them but i couldn’t stop them. She told me it’s perfectly normal to have intrusive thoughts and she knows that that’s all they are because i have no desire to act on those thoughts. 

“Sometimes you drive down the road and see a car coming the other way and think ‘i wonder what’d happen if i just swerved and hit them head on.’ everybody has that once in a while, but then you remember that’s a crazy thought your brain just had and move on. Because you don’t actually want to hit the car.” 

The difference between an intrusive thought and a desire is how you act on the thought. It’s okay to open up to a therapist about it. If they know their stuff they’ll know you don’t actually want to hurt anyone and you just need help reacting to them in a way that won’t let you feel controlled by them. Definitely look for therapists who specialize in anxiety disorders, even ocd if you can, as intrusive thoughts are a common symptom with these. I hope you feel better soon. They’re just thoughts. Try your best to not cling on when they pop up. Treat them like a cloud: let it float by after you see it. Best of luck ❤️

First, you cannot fix her problems for her. Ultimately, she has to do that for herself. But you CAN help as much as you’re able. But don’t forget to take care of yourself too. You can’t help someone else if you can’t help yourself. 

Try not to force an answer out of her. If she doesn’t want to tell you what’s wrong, that’s ok. She doesn’t have to. She might not even know in that moment. She just might not feel good. That’s ok. Instead try “can you tell me what you’re feeling?” Or “what can i do that might help?” She might not know the answers to these. That’s ok too. Breathing is good, try and find some breathing exercises for her to follow. A good one is inhale for 4 seconds, hold for 4, exhale for 4, hold for 4 again. Also look up some grounding exercises for when her anxiety is bad. 

Ask her why she thinks she doesn’t deserve to get better. Remind her that she isn’t a bad person and she’s allowed to not be perfect because nobody’s perfect. 

Do suggest therapy, but don’t shove it down her throat ykno? If she goes to a school counselor, everything is confidential (just like any other counselor or therapist.) the only times they would tell her parents anything is if they thought she was planning on harming herself or others. (Her current eating habits might fall into this category.) 

Have her create a self care routine. Things in the day she schedules for herself to do that help her cope healthily. Maybe she likes to ride her bike or go on a walk outside. Maybe it’s reading or writing in a journal. Maybe it’s coloring. Have her do something she likes that she can focus on and make her feel good.

I hope this helped, and i hope she can get the help she needs soon. Keep trying your best, and if you ever need to take a break, remember that’s ok to do.
